title: Director Paul Wright Pushes George MacKay to the Edge in ‘Mission’: ‘How Do You Feel Something When You’ve Been Numbed to the Modern World?’
description:
For Scottish director Paul Wright, “Mission” began with a feeling.

	“For the first time with a film I’ve made, it was kind of tapping into a feelin
body:
For Scottish director Paul Wright, “Mission” began with a feeling.

	“For the first time with a film I’ve made, it was kind of tapping into a feeling,” he tells Variety. “More so than plot or story, it was just that feeling that some of us get sometimes of feeling maybe disconnected from the world and feeling you need more. You need something more.”

	Starring George MacKay as Dylan, an alienated man who pushes himself toward increasingly extreme experiences in a bid to evade death, “Mission” will have its world premiere in competition at Edinburgh Intl. Film Festival. Rosy McEwen co-stars as his estranged sister Claire.
	

	The film is backed by BBC Film, Screen Scotland and Ffilm Cymru Wales with National Lottery funding. A co-production between Early Day Films and 65 Wilding Films, it was developed with Screen Scotland and BBC Film. Producers are Kate Byers, Linn Waite, Alex Thiele, Marie-Elena Dyche and Lowri Roberts, while Blue Finch Films handles worldwide sales.


	For Wright, Dylan’s increasingly dangerous behavior grew out of a romantic ideal: the desire for an “all or nothing” existence.

	“There’s that contrast of what he’s feeling and this desire for sensation, and I think within that it can slide from light to dark quite simply,” Wright says. “Where do you stop? What’s the limit?”

	Dylan’s desire to feel and to live propels him toward the anarchic.

	“In this kind of uber-capitalist world we live in, we’ve all fallen into certain patterns that, for a lot of people, aren’t fulfilling,” Wright says.
	

	As traditional religion has declined and work, money and capitalism have occupied more of that space, Wright became interested in a culture of “just surviving, just getting by.”

	“How do you feel something when you’ve been kind of numbed to the modern world?”

	The film pushes Dylan toward what Wright calls the “thin line between transcendence and transgression.”



	

					Director Paul Wright on set
	



	“It becomes a kind of epic within one character: all or nothing, heaven or hell,” he says. “How far do you go, and where do you stop, when your goal is a feeling?”

	Music, movement and Dylan’s body take on an almost ritualistic function as he searches for sensation.

	“It is tapping into trying to reach a level of ecstasy or rapture,” Wright says. “That primal energy maybe a lot of us have moved away from.”

	That impulse has roots beyond cinema. Wright drew inspiration from performance artists including Chris Burden and Marina Abramović, as well as Dadaism and the alternative music he discovered while growing up in a small village in Fife.

	Encountering work outside the mainstream could feel “almost like a religious experience,” he recalls.

	“Oh my God, that really connects with me in a way that nothing has before,” Wright says. “It became this almost obsession to seek out this alternative culture.”

	He sees outsider figures such as radical performance artists as “modern-day shamans,” willing to disturb accepted patterns in the hope of revealing another way of living.

	“Sometimes it can become uncomfortable when someone rubs up against that, or challenges that,” he says.

	Dylan ultimately directs that challenge inward.

	“He feels he has to go as far as he possibly can to complete his own journey,” Wright says. “It’s about that challenge of the self and going into his own darkness.”

	But “Mission” also gives Dylan an emotional tether in Claire. McEwen, who broke out in “Blue Jean,” plays the estranged sister whose presence reconnects him with childhood and an earlier sense of possibility, before the constraints of adulthood began to close in.



	

					Rosy McEwan as Claire in “Mission”
									Diana Patient
	



	“There was a simplicity in the world,” Wright says. “It felt anything was possible at that stage, compared to the modern world kind of beating them down over the years.”
	

	Claire grew in importance during the making of the film, becoming both a counterpoint to Dylan and its emotional anchor.

	“They’re both the same side in some ways. They’re both struggling,” Wright says. “There are things we all need, connection and meaning.”

	“Mission” reunites Wright and MacKay more than a decade after “For Those in Peril,” Wright’s feature debut, which premiered in Cannes Critics’ Week.

	“Obviously I knew what George would give us, that he would give us his all,” Wright says.

	Wright’s 2017 archive documentary “Arcadia” also shaped his approach to “Mission,” reinforcing his conviction about what cinema can do beyond conventional storytelling.

	“I do see film as a sensory medium, and this idea of trying to create emotions through images and sounds excites me more than anything in cinema,” he says.

	“It’s not about A to B to C plot progression.”

	Instead, “Mission” moves vertically into Dylan’s psyche, where memory, dreams, fear, imagination and reality begin to merge.

	“They become these different streams of consciousness within a single character,” Wright says. “Maybe not discerning too much on which is which. It becomes this quite immersive experience, hopefully, for the viewer.”

	Shot in and around Glasgow in 2024, the film also gave Wright the opportunity to foreground the city as a specifically Scottish setting.

	“It has a character of its own. Its own personality,” he says.

	After a lengthy gap between narrative features, Wright is now developing several projects, and wants to push the instincts behind “Mission” even further.

	“There’s something that I’m trying to explore in film,” he says. “How far can I push things to get to the things that I’m most interested in exploring?”

	He is aware that this work is not conventional. For Wright, that is part of its value.

	“Sometimes it is that stuff that is one step outside,” he says. “My hope is that the people that do connect with it really connect with it.”

schema.headline: Director Paul Wright Pushes George MacKay to the Edge in ‘Mission’: ‘How Do You Feel Something When You’ve Been Numbed to the Modern World?’

title: Black Women Earned Record Emmy Directing Noms as Asian Auteurs Made Gains. Will Wins Follow?
description:
One of the most consequential storylines of this Emmy season involves the ones who say, “Action!”

	Black women hold five directing nominations acro
body:
One of the most consequential storylines of this Emmy season involves the ones who say, “Action!”

	Black women hold five directing nominations across three categories this year, the most the Television Academy has ever recognized in a single cycle. Salli Richardson-Whitfield is nominated twice in drama directing, for HBO Max’s “The Gilded Age” and “Task,” alongside Hanelle Culpepper for the Hulu dystopian thriller “Paradise.” Ricki Hughes earned a nod for helming the variety special “Dave Chappelle: The Unstoppable,” and Alexandria Stapleton is nominated for the documentary series “Sean Combs: The Reckoning,” both from Netflix.
	

	To understand why five is a number worth stopping on, you must count backward.


	Debbie Allen became the first Black woman nominated for an Emmy in directing in any genre category, for “The Debbie Allen Special,” in 1989. It took 20 years for another to follow: Millicent Shelton, for the “30 Rock” episode “Kidney Now!” in 2009.

	What came after was less like a gusher and more like a trickle: Laurie Ann Gibson for the special “Lady Gaga Presents the Monster Ball Tour: At Madison Square Garden” in 2011; Dee Rees for the HBO movie “Bessie” in 2015; Beyoncé Knowles-Carter for “Lemonade” in 2016 and again for “Homecoming: A Film By Beyoncé” in 2019; Ava DuVernay for the documentary “13th” in 2017 and the limited series “When They See Us” in 2019; Nadia Hallgren for “Becoming” in 2020; Michaela Coel for “I May Destroy You” in 2021; Dime Davis and Bridget Stokes for “A Black Lady Sketch Show” in 2021 and 2022; Nneka Onuorah for the Prime Video competition series “Lizzo’s Watch Out for the Big Grrrls” in 2022. 
	

	Richardson-Whitfield scored in 2024 with the one and only season of HBO’s “Winning Time: The Rise of the Lakers Dynasty,” which made her the first woman of color nominated in drama directing.

	That is 35 years of names rattled off in one single breath. However, five in one morning is showing that progress is being made, even when it seems like Hollywood and the studio and network system is stepping away from DEI.



	

	



	But when you look at how many have won, that’s a tougher pill to swallow.

	The only Black women to walk off with the statuette are Stokes and Onuorah, both in variety. Drama, comedy, limited series and documentary have never produced one.

	Which is what gives some of this year’s nominees some hope. Stapleton’s bid in particular could have the best shot at going the distance. “Sean Combs: The Reckoning” arrives with the timeliest subject on the documentary ballot and, by most reads of the race, the best shot at putting a Black woman onstage in September, especially with the backing of the streaming giant and critical acclaim the series received.

	Directing nominations function as hiring credentials in a way acting nominations do not. Showrunners staff from lists, agents build those lists from recognition and a name that has never appeared on one is a name that has to be argued and fought for in every room.

	The Asian American column is thinner still. Cary Joji Fukunaga won in drama in 2014 for the first season of “True Detective.” Lee Sung Jin won in limited series for “Beef.” And that completes the list.



	

					Beef. Creator/Showrunner/Director/Executive Producer Lee Sung Jin in episode 101 of Beef. Cr. Andrew Cooper/Netflix © 2023
									ANDREW COOPER/NETFLIX
	



	Lee is back this cycle with the Netflix anthology’s sophomore season, which pulled 16 nominations overall (the most of any miniseries) and three for Lee himself. And Hiro Murai, now holding 11 career Emmy nominations and one win as an executive producer on the first season of “The Bear,” is triple-nominated for Apple TV’s horror-comedy “Widow’s Bay.” He is widely read as one of the front-runners in comedy directing. A win would make him the first Asian director to take that category and only the third Asian director to win in any directing category in Emmy history.

	Murai doesn’t pretend the number means nothing.
	

	“The significance of that is not lost on me,” he tells Variety. “Having been someone who came up in this industry not seeing a lot of Asian folks that I could sort of model after, I understand the importance of feature directors of Asian descent knowing that this was possible.”

	Murai, who arrived in the United States from Japan at 9 years old, offered a theory on why there has been such an absence of Asian representation. “You accept the representation that you get, and then you adapt to what’s presented to you,” he reflects. “Asian filmmakers in America probably haven’t seen a lot of Asian filmmakers represented, and you internalize that. You think that’s not a position that you can reach.”

	He also pushes back on the assumption that diverse authorship requires diverse subject matter, a framing that has quietly narrowed what directors of color get offered. Neither “Atlanta” nor “Widow’s Bay” is his story on the surface.



	

					Apple Studios
									Apple Studios
	



	“Like all creative collaborations, I saw something in it that I could plug myself into,” Murai explains. “My participation in these stories can be part of diverse storytelling or Asian storytelling even if it’s not about Asian characters.”

	Lee puts it out more bluntly.

	“You always have to prove yourself tenfold more than your peers to be noticed, to be given another chance,” he shares. “I’ve been that way my whole life, and I think that is true of any creative of color.”

	All of this is happening inside contraction. By Lee’s count, 46 fewer shows went into production in 2026. DEI initiatives that were announced with press releases in 2020 have retired without them.

	“I think it is the hiring, and also diversifying the Academy and the peer groups,” Lee explains. “There’s been a lot of progress for sure. Certainly, it has changed since I started, but that doesn’t mean we slow down.”

	Lee argues that visibility functions as infrastructure, not sentiment.

	“Wanting to be in this field and see a face that looks like mine on television is not a stereotype,” he shares, citing the comedy classic “Harold and Kumar Go to White Castle” with John Cho and Kal Penn as a revelation for a younger version of himself. “I think these little moments do stack.”

	Lee says he intends to keep hiring against the trend through his overall Netflix deal, and even beyond that, proven by his executive producer credit on “Lurker,” the directorial debut of former “Beef” writer Alex Russell.
	

	“It’ll never not be a priority for me,” he says, “and I just hope it becomes a priority for other people too.”

	For Murai, he’s looking past September.

	“There’s forward movement, backward movement, but the overarching shape is that we’re heading in the right direction,” he says. “I see a lot of young filmmakers from completely different backgrounds interested in telling stories. That’s so exciting to me, more so than when I was a kid going to film school.”

	No matter how hard people try, you can’t get rid of the color in Hollywood.

schema.headline: Black Women Earned Record Emmy Directing Noms as Asian Auteurs Made Gains. Will Wins Follow?

title: If Paramount Leaves California, It Might Cut Costs but Wouldn’t Save on State Taxes
description: Paramount is threatening to leave California if it cannot reach a deal with Attorney General Rob Bonta to allow it to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery
body:
Paramount is threatening to leave California if it cannot reach a deal with Attorney General Rob Bonta to allow it to acquire Warner Bros. Discovery.

	Puck reported the threat on Tuesday, following a similar report in Semafor last month, and adding that Paramount CEO David Ellison believes the move would save the company $500 million a year in taxes. The figure is meant to make the play both more credible and more threatening, quantifying both what Paramount stands to gain and what California stands to lose.
	

	But moving out of California would not reduce the company’s tax bill by anything close to that, according to experts and financial statements. For one thing, the company’s state tax liability is far closer to zero than to half a billion dollars. And for another, relocating its headquarters wouldn’t actually change its tax bill.


	“The effect on corporation tax is going to be pretty minimal,” said Rowan Isaaks, an economist with the California Legislative Analyst’s Office, a nonpartisan advisory body. “The location of your employees does not factor into how we calculate corporation tax liability. So even if they did move most of their jobs somewhere else, it wouldn’t affect corporation tax.”

	Paramount appears to be basing its estimate on the expectation of a generous incentive package from whatever state it moves to. It may also be factoring in the proceeds from the potential sale of the Paramount lot, which is likely worth a few billion dollars, as well as lower overhead if it relocates to a state with a substantially lower cost of living.

	But those potential savings have nothing to do with California tax policy, and would not represent a loss to the state’s coffers. To the extent that jobs leave the state, the state would lose personal income tax from those employees, but Paramount would likely have to retain a substantial workforce in the state to continue to do business in the film and TV industry.
	

	California is often tagged as a hostile to business due to high taxes and regulations. Other companies, including Tesla and Oracle, have contributed to the narrative by relocating their headquarters elsewhere. 

	But state corporation taxes are apportioned based on where customers are located, not on where the company is based, as Isaaks explained in a report published on Tuesday. California taxes the share of Paramount’s income that comes from California-based advertisers, distributors, Paramount+ subscribers, and so on. That share would not change even if the location of the headquarters changed.

	“When I’ve done the analysis of the tax savings of moving out of California, for most companies that are not flow-through [i.e., not partnerships or LLCs], there really isn’t an income tax savings,” said Robert Johnson, a CPA who teaches state and local taxes at Cal State University Northridge. “California is market-based sourcing. Unless you’re going to get all your customers to move, you’re not going to change how much gets sourced to California.”

	Even more to the point, Paramount Skydance doesn’t pay anything like $500 million in state taxes to begin with. Public companies are not required to report how much they pay each state, but they do report their overall state and local tax liability.

	And according to its most recent annual report, Paramount Skydance and its predecessor, Paramount Global, got a net tax benefit — not a bill — of $11 million from state and local governments in 2025. (The majority of its state and local tax effect came from six states: Pennsylvania, New York, California, New Jersey, Ohio, and Oregon.)

	Like other states, California regularly provides Paramount and CBS with millions in tax credits to make films and TV shows in the state. Some studios have far more California credits than they can use because they do not owe enough taxes. Paramount was among the companies that persuaded the state to make film credits refundable starting last year.

	Paramount does pay property tax on its studio lot. But the lot is currently appraised at $331 million — a bargain compared to its potential market value — which works out to an annual tax bill of about $6 million. If Paramount were to sell the lot, it would incur significant transfer taxes and capital gains taxes, likely dwarfing any property tax savings.
	

	To the extent that Paramount employees move out of California to a lower-tax state, they would save on their personal income taxes, with the highest earners realizing the greatest savings. That wouldn’t help Paramount, but the company could save money by paying workers less in a state with a lower cost of living, which would also reduce its payroll tax bill, and by paying less for outside services.

	A source familiar with Paramount’s analysis said that corporate taxes are not where it expects to reap the greatest savings. The company declined to comment.

schema.headline: If Paramount Leaves California, It Might Cut Costs but Wouldn’t Save on State Taxes

title: ‘Deli Boys’ Canceled After Two Seasons at Hulu, Onyx Collective
description:
The comedy series “Deli Boys” has been canceled at Hulu after two seasons, Variety has confirmed. 

	The series, which aired under Hulu’s Onyx Colle
body:
The comedy series “Deli Boys” has been canceled at Hulu after two seasons, Variety has confirmed. 

	The series, which aired under Hulu’s Onyx Collective brand, starred Asif Ali, Saagar Shaikh, and Poorna Jagannathan. Fred Armisen joined the show in its second season along with Andrew Rannells, with Brian George once again appearing as Ahmad and Jake Prizant playing Matthew. Kumail Nanjiani, Lilly Singh, Robin Thede, and returning guest star Tan France also appeared in Season 2. 
	

	The show was popular with critics, with the two seasons averaging a 98% critical approval rating on Rotten Tomatoes. It failed to find a wide enough audience, however, to justify a third season. 


	The official logline for Season 2 stated: 

	“Turns out inheriting a criminal empire was the easy part… and more money really does mean more problems. This season on ‘Deli Boys,’ the Dars are drowning in dirty cash and Philly’s sketchiest crooks are circling. Enter Max Sugar (Armisen): casino king, money launderer, and Lucky’s new crush who turns laundering into a chaotic situationship. Raj (Shaikh) plots revenge on Ahmad, Mir tries to expand DarCo without blowing it up, and Philly D.A. Andrew Chadwater hopes one big bust will make him mayor.”

	The series has now ended on a cliffhanger with no resolution. As the second season came to an end, the boys and Lucky come out on top, but they receive a note from “the eldest Dar,” who warns they are coming to take their piece of Baba’s fortune.

	Who was that other Dar sibling might be? Ali had a theory.

	“Robert Downey Jr., but he still plays Doom,” he joked. “It’s part of the multiverse.”
	

	Abdullah Saeed created “Deli Boys,” which was developed by Jenni Konner and Nora Silver under Jenni Konner Productions. Michelle Nader served as showrunner and was an executive producer alongside Saeed, Konner and Silver. The series hailed from Onyx Collective and was produced by 20th Television.

	Deadline first reported the cancellation.

schema.headline: ‘Deli Boys’ Canceled After Two Seasons at Hulu, Onyx Collective

title: ‘Stuart Fails to Save the Universe’ Renewed for Season 2 at HBO Max
description:
The “Big Bang Theory” spinoff “Stuart Fails to Save the Universe” has been renewed for Season 2 at HBO Max. 

	The news comes after the series has a
body:
The “Big Bang Theory” spinoff “Stuart Fails to Save the Universe” has been renewed for Season 2 at HBO Max. 

	The news comes after the series has aired just four episodes of its 10-episode first season. The series originally premiered at the streamer on July 23. 

	“We’re delighted with how this hilarious, genre-bending show from Chuck, Zak, and Bill has connected with the audience, both devotees of ‘The Big Bang Theory’ and new fans alike,” said Amy Gravitt, EVP of  HBO Programming and Head of HBO & HBO Max Comedy Series. “Along with everyone else, we can’t wait to see the worlds they conjure for these beloved characters next season.”
	

	“Stuart Fails to Save the Universe” hails from creators Chuck Lorre, Zak Penn, and Bill Prady. Lorre and Prady previously co-created “The Big Bang Theory.” The new show stars “Big Bang Theory” alums Kevin Sussman, Lauren Lapkus, Brian Posehn, and John Ross Bowie. A number of other stars of the original show appear in guest star roles. 


	The logline for the show states, “Comic book store owner Stuart Bloom (Sussman) is tasked with restoring reality after he breaks a device built by Sheldon and Leonard, accidentally bringing about a multiverse Armageddon. Stuart is aided in this quest by his girlfriend Denise (Lapkus), geologist friend Bert (Posehn), and quantum physicist/all-around pain in the ass Barry Kripke (Bowie). Along the way, they meet alternate-universe versions of characters we’ve come to know and love from ‘The Big Bang Theory.’ As the title implies, things don’t go well.” 

	“Stuart Fails to Save the Universe” is produced by Chuck Lorre Productions in association with Warner Bros. Television, where Lorre is under an overall deal. Lorre, Penn, and Prady are also executive producers. Kyle Newacheck directed multiple episodes and executive produces.
	

	“Chuck, Zak, and Bill delivered something truly special with ‘Stuart Fails to Save the Universe’ — a completely original take on one of the most beloved franchises of all time that captures the unique essence that made ‘The Big Bang Theory’ so special,” said Channing Dungey, chairman and CEO of Warner Bros. Television Group and WBD US Networks. “It’s been an absolute joy to see audiences embrace this next iteration so passionately, and we can’t wait to continue exploring the multiverse in season two.” 

	This is the fourth show in the “Big Bang Theory” universe. Aside from the mothership show, which ran for 12 highly-rated seasons on CBS, the prequel “Young Sheldon” wrapped up its own seven-season run at the broadcast network in May 2024. A spinoff of that show, “Georgie & Mandy’s First Marriage” starring Montana Jordan and Emily Osment, debuted on CBS on Oct. 17, 2024.

schema.headline: ‘Stuart Fails to Save the Universe’ Renewed for Season 2 at HBO Max

title: Squishmallows Movie in the Works at Amazon MGM (EXCLUSIVE)
description: Your moviegoing experience is about to get a lot plusher. Squishmallows, the popular collectible toys known for softness and irreverent personalitie
body:
Your moviegoing experience is about to get a lot plusher. Squishmallows, the popular collectible toys known for softness and irreverent personalities, will come to life in a new feature film.

	Variety can report that Amazon MGM is developing a tentpole family film around the brand, licensing rights and co-producing with creator Jazwares. The studio is partnering with uberproducer Beau Flynn (“Moana,” “Hello Kitty”), with Shelby Thomas overseeing for the FlynnPictureCo banner.
	

	Amazon MGM went big for the deal, insiders say, and want to create global-facing, four-quadrant event with Flynn. It’s presently unknown if the film will be animated, live-action or a hybrid. Creative attachments have yet to be revealed.


	Squishmallows was launched in 2017 and has evolved into a billion-dollar venture across 60 countries. Stakeholders estimate that two of the toys are sold per second. The product range spans a universe of over 3,000 original character, from ambassador Cam the Cat to Bigfoots, Axolotls and an adorable sentient grilled cheese named Lil Gouda. The toys have cross-generational appeal, as well, hooking kids, teens, adults and the collector market. Over 600 million have been sold to date.  The range is also leveraged for licensing in categories like apparel, health and beauty and home décor. The toys signed with CAA in 2021.

	Flynn has a knack for broad IP, having delivered films like “Moana” and “Jungle Cruise” at Disney. He’s also dabbled in hard action with “Black Adam” and Netflix’s top-viewed “Red Notice.” He’s currently at work on Warner Bros.’ “Hello Kitty” animated film, set to hit theaters in July 2028.

schema.headline: Squishmallows Movie in the Works at Amazon MGM (EXCLUSIVE)

title: After the YA Drama ‘Sterling Point’ Topped the Prime Video Charts, What’s Next for LuckyChap TV?
description: If the YA drama “Sterling Point” has become your new hyper-fixation show, you’re not alone.Amazon reports that the coming-of-age series, from creato
body:
If the YA drama “Sterling Point” has become your new hyper-fixation show, you’re not alone.Amazon reports that the coming-of-age series, from creator Megan Park, was the most-watched show on Prime Video worldwide since its Aug. 5 debut.

	“Sterling Point” centers on 17-year-old Annie Jacobson (Ella Rubin, best known for “The Idea of You”), who was raised in New York City with her twin brother (Keen Ruffalo) by her adoptive father (Jay Duplass). But when the twins’ grandfather dies and they inherit his picturesque island, Annie sets out for Muskoka, Canada, to learn more. What, or who, she finds is Ramona (Amélie Hoeferle), a standoffish girl who looks just like Annie’s late mother and insists Gordon was also her granddad. The series unfolds over a sun-drenched summer as the two young women develop a sisterly bond while navigating all sorts of drama in the romance department (It wouldn’t be a YA series if there wasn’t at least one love triangle!) and more family secrets are revealed.
	

	Variety’s review was a rave, with TV critic Aramide Tinubu pointing out how “Sterling Point” offers something “wholly unique and wistfully authentic” to the YA genre — populated by such hits as “The Summer I Turned Pretty,” “Off Campus” and “Every Year After” on the same streamer. What sets this show apart, Tinubu writes, is the depth of its exploration into themes of “grief, self-discovery and being brave enough to face the past.”


	The success of “Sterling Point” doesn’t surprise the team behind it as much as it delights them.“We made this show for audiences, so to have audiences begin to engage with and hopefully gravitate toward the things that were really important to us in the telling of it, and to see themselves reflected in the storytelling and the characters,” executive producer Dani Gorin tells Variety over Zoom. “That’s what it’s all about.”
	

	Gorin leads the TV division at LuckyChap, the company behind “Wuthering Heights,” “Promising Young Woman,” “I, Tonya” and the $1.4 billion-grossing blockbuster, “Barbie.” LuckyChap also produced Park’s second feature, “My Old Ass,” which was where their professional love affair with the filmmaker (who began her career as a teen star on shows like “The Secret Life of the American Teenager”) and the Canadian island of Muskoka (where Park spent summers growing up) began.

	The “repeat business” with Park is just one of the elements that makes “Sterling Point” the epitome of a LuckyChap show. The company has been in the TV business since 2019, launching with the Hulu comedy “Dollface,” then going on to produce acclaimed limited series like Netflix’s “Maid.”



	

					Josh Schwartz, Raffi Donatich, Megan Park, Dani Gorin and Anna Beben on the set of “Sterling Point.”
									Sabrina Lantos/Prime
	



	This time last year, Gorin was gearing up for the launch of “Sirens” — their second series with creator “Maid” creator Molly Smith Metzler — and visiting the set of “Sterling Point,” which featured “The O.C.” and “Gossip Girl” alums Josh Schwartz and Stephanie Savage as co-showrunners.

	“Being in Muskoka with everyone — the cast, the crew — it’s such a special place, and it does have like a camp sort of feel,” Gorin recalls. “We had days where we would be shooting on the water, and you’d be jet-skiing over to a camera boat, and you’re like, ‘This is work?’”

	But for all the fun in the sun, Gorin and her six-person team were simultaneously working on their next few shows. “We were getting ready to start the writers’ room on ‘Life is Strange’ in London, and we were working on the pilot script for ‘Sex Criminals,’” she says. “And we were starting to think about ‘Retrievals,’ which is our next show with [Metzler].”

	Louie Hayes, who oversaw the day-to-day on “Sterling Point,” is now focused on “Sex Criminals,” the live-action adaptation of the popular comic book series written by Matt Fraction and illustrated by Chip Zdarsky for Amazon. Imogen Poots will star as Suze, a “normal girl with an extraordinary ability: when she has sex, she stops time.” One night, the logline explains, Suze meets Jon (John Reynolds), who has the same gift. “And so they do what any other sex having, time stopping couple would do: they rob banks.”
	

	Kumail Nanjiani, Emily V. Gordon and Tze Chun developed the series, produced by LuckyChap and Winter Coat Films, with Nia DaCosta directing multiple episodes and joining the team as an executive producer.

	“What I love about ‘Sex Criminals’ is how specific it feels to the people making it,” writes Hayes in an email from the New York set. “Building off what Matt and Chip created in the comic, Emily, Kumail, and Tze are taking this big, provocative, high-concept idea and making something only they could make — a show that’s funny, idiosyncratic, and ambitious with an enormous amount of heart. It’s such a surprising way into something so romantic and life-affirming.”

	Meanwhile, Natalie Berkus is across the country in Vancouver for production on “Life Is Strange,” a sci-fi mystery drama, based on the hit video game. The series follows photography student Max Caulfield (newcomer Tatum Grace Hopkins), who gains the ability to rewind time while saving her best friend, Chloe Price (Maisy Stella). Max and Chloe then work together to explore the town of Arcadia Bay and solve the disappearance of Chloe’s friend, Rachel Amber (Esther McGregor).

	Charlie Covell will serve as showrunner for the series, which is a co-production between LuckyChap, Square Enix, Story Kitchen and Amazon MGM Studios. Karyn Kusama will direct the first two episodes and executive produce.

	“What I love about ‘Life is Strange’ is that it’s a big and operatic idea based on beloved IP, but the thematic foundation of the show that Charlie has so brilliantly crafted is rooted entirely in the emotional truths of the characters,” Berkus says. “It’s a really exciting foray into opening up the aperture of our brand and challenging ourselves to explore new types of stories and worlds while always coming back to the authenticity of our artists and what they want to tell.”

	Gorin also notes that “Life is Strange” is a game where, unlike most, 50% of the audience who plays it are women.

	“If you’ve played ‘Life is Strange,’ it really does lend itself to this sort of long-form storytelling. That’s such a unique and exciting challenge for us. It’s something that we did with ‘Barbie.’ We feel there’s a big opportunity there if the source material is treated with that sort of reverence and care,” she says. “Everyone who’s part of making the show is a fan of the game. There are so many Easter eggs and little nods that the eagle-eyed fans are going to be so excited about.”
	

	Casting Stella in the lead role is also an Easter egg of sorts, and it proves that “repeat business” extends to all the company’s creative relationships, not just filmmakers.

	“Megan is such a superstar with casting. It is one of her superpowers,” Gorin says. “I don’t know if she gets enough credit for this, but Megan helped break Jenna Ortega in ‘The Fallout’ and Stella in ‘My Old Ass,’ and I think this cast that she has assembled for ‘Sterling Point’ really are the next generation of big stars.”



	

					Maisy Stella stars in LuckyChap’s upcoming series “Life is Strange.”
									Earl Gibson III/Deadline
	



	Like Stella, LuckyChap is keeping star Emilia Jones on their talent roster after she starred in their upcoming film “Bad Bridget,” opposite Alison Oliver. News broke Thursday that Jones will star in “Retrievals,” the Netflix limited series, based on the New York Times and Serial Productions podcast of the same name.

	Per the logline, the show follows an “unlikely community of IVF patients who come together to crusade against Yale University after they are operated on without anesthesia — because a nurse stole their fentanyl.” Jones will play Gabby Clemente, described as “a New Haven bartender and student teacher whose life is upended by her traumatic egg retrieval surgery. Upon discovering that a nurse at the clinic was stealing vast amounts of fentanyl, Gabby seeks out other victims and leads a groundbreaking legal battle.”

	The opportunity to work with Metzler again was at the top of the LuckyChap team’s list of reasons to produce the series, but there’s also a more meaningful aftereffect.

	“It’s an opportunity to shine a light on a really insidious systemic failure in the medical space, which is the way that women’s pain is routinely dismissed and ignored, and the standard of care is different for women,” Gorin says about the storyline. “It’s a really hard thing to talk about and to showcase, and the podcast did that so brilliantly.”

	She continues: “The opportunity to tell stories that can have an impact is such a privilege. It’s something ‘Maid’ did as it related to what domestic violence could look like. We never are issue driven for the sake of it. But when we’re able to move the conversation in and around those sorts of things, it’s really meaningful.”
	

	Considering all these different genres, one might wonder, what makes something a LuckyChap show?

	“Part of what makes the brand so strong is that there is a shared vision across film and TV: it really comes down to supporting artists and their vision,” Gorin says. “Our brand definitely is about female stories and/or storytellers, but that works across genres.”

	Another key factor is that the idea feels truly authored. “That is something that helps cut through for an audience because you can feel that you can feel a voice, you can feel a point of view,” she says. “Only this person could have done this in this way; it’s so very much in their voice, which I think is rare in television, actually, just given what the medium is and how it’s typically made.”

	The final ingredient is finding fresh stories that feel “a little bit left of center” tonally. Gorin explains that they aim to produce projects “that have something to say but aren’t being didactic in the way that we’re saying it and aren’t force-feeding an audience a message, but rather, engaging in a dialogue with them and giving them things to chew on and sit with.”

	“Sterling Point” hasn’t officially been renewed by Amazon yet, but rest assured that Park and LuckyChap are invested in telling more of this story. In fact, the show represents the company’s first step toward more ongoing series after enjoying success making limited series.

	“It is a different calculus than building a limited series,” Gorin says, but creating series that could continue for multiple seasons was a big priority for her team. “’Sterling Point,’ ‘Sex Criminals’ and ‘Life is Strange’ are meant to be ongoing. There’s a lot in the pipeline.”

	Another point of pride is that all those shows have female filmmakers at the center: from Park with “Sterling Point” and Nicole Kassell with “Sirens” to DaCosta (“Sex Criminals”), Kusama (“Life is Strange”) and Lila Neugebauer (“Retrievals”). “It very much represents the ethos of the company,” Gorin says.

	With so many projects in the works, what could the LuckyChap team possibly do next?

	“We are really interested in and excited by the music space and feel like there’s a big opportunity there in television,” Gorin says, teasing that the company is developing a mystery project with a “musical component.”
	

	“I’m Glad My Mom Died,” based on Jennette McCurdy’s bestselling memoir, is still in development at Apple TV. Plus, LuckyChap is working on a family drama, which is a project close to Gorin’s heart.

	“’Six Feet Under’ was my absolute favorite show, and probably the reason I work in television,” she says. “It’s something I’ve never done and the company’s never done, and that’s definitely a big target for us.”

	So, as the old TV saying goes, “Tune in next week.” It probably won’t be the same time or the same channel, but for LuckyChap, the same success feels inevitable.

schema.headline: After the YA Drama ‘Sterling Point’ Topped the Prime Video Charts, What’s Next for LuckyChap TV?

	Sports fans won’t have to rely on cable anymore to catch the big games and tournaments this fall, as streaming service DIRECTV launches a new promo for cord cutters looking to take in the action.

	DIRECTV has dropped the price of its MySports Genre Pack down to $49.99 for your first month of service (regularly $64.99/month). That’s a one-time savings of 23% off.

	The MySports Genre Pack offers more than 20 live sports and broadcast networks that you can stream online, including ESPN, ESPN2, FS1, TBS and TNT. Subscribers also get access to premium sports channels like MLB Network, NFL Network, NBA TV, and Tennis Channel. Those channels are not typically included in streaming packages and are often priced as add-ons, so this DIRECTV deal is worth taking advantage of. 
	

	Even better: DIRECTV’s MySports Genre Pack also includes a full subscription ESPN Unlimited Plan, the sporting network’s standalone streaming service. Pricing for ESPN Unlimited Plan — which offers live sports, documentaries and specials – normally runs $29.99/month on its own, but DIRECTV subscribers can get the streaming app included in their sports package. 

	In addition to the sports channels, the package also includes a live feed of the ABC, CBS, FOX and NBC local affiliates in your region (where available). The new DIRECTV promo gets you access to the MySports Genre Pack for just $49.99 for your first month of service. Pricing renews at the $64.99/month standard rate following your first 30 days (and after your free five-day trial).

	The deal comes as Major League Baseball heads into playoff season, and the NBA, NFL and NHL are preparing to start up again. You’ll also get access to college football season, in addition to upcoming tennis tournaments like the U.S. Open.
	

	For more information on the MySports promo, go to directv.com/affiliates/genre-packs.

title: ‘Pretty Babies’ Director Tyler-Marie Evans on Sex Work, Female Friendship and Finding Humanity Beyond Stereotypes
description: We all have souls. That sentiment sits at the heart of “Pretty Babies,” Tyler-Marie Evans‘ feature debut, which world premieres Friday in competitio
body:
We all have souls. That sentiment sits at the heart of “Pretty Babies,” Tyler-Marie Evans‘ feature debut, which world premieres Friday in competition at the Edinburgh Intl. Film Festival. The project attracted Jordan Wagner from Wagner Entertainment and also independent film icon Christine Vachon‘s Killer Films, who alongside star Ashley Benson took on producer roles. 

	It follows Marie and Luna, played by Emily Alyn Lind and Sadie Stanley as best friends who set off to chase a dream and escape their trauma only to take paths into sex work and oblivion. 
	

	“There’s been a lot said on the topic of sex work, especially in cinema,” Evans told Variety. “I felt like I hadn’t seen this topic discussed in an interior way.”


	“This is a film about what happens when you disassociate from your body, and you no longer are in touch with your body, and yet the world is placing questions upon you. ‘Are you the whore? Are you the virgin? Are you good? Are you bad?'”

	For the director, those questions arrive long before women are able to answer them themselves. Sexuality and identity become intertwined, while the complexity of a person is reduced to categories that culture, including cinema, repeats. 

	“Pretty Babies” avoids framing those choices as either tragedy or liberation. 

	“I really wanted to show it through the sisterhood,” she said.

	Marie and Luna’s world expands with the arrival of Sapphire (Ashley Benson) and Gemma (Madelaine Petsch), whose relationship mirrors many of the same tensions.



	

	



	Before writing the film, Evans interviewed women involved in sex work and found herself drawn to relationships that swerve simple moral definitions.
	

	“I saw a lot of friendships where one person was desperately hurting the other, and yet it was the only space that they found love and connection,” she said. “There’s this weird tug of war between connection and being seen.”

	That complexity extends to the film’s central relationship between Marie and Luna. Luna repeatedly hurts Marie, yet remains someone she loves and often needs. There is a mirroring in the relationship of Sapphire and Gemma whereby Sapphire seems to have a hold over Gemma while also having a strong bond.

	“I’m sort of tired of the same type of story of a woman being saved by a man,” Evans explained. “I didn’t want to show these perfect friendships or perfect relationships. I wanted to show the darkness and the complexity.”

	Luna herself was partly inspired by Edie Sedgwick. Evans became fascinated by Andy Warhol’s descriptions of Sedgwick refusing to wash, choosing instead to repeatedly apply makeup.

	“I wanted to show the world Luna came from,” Evans said. “I never wanted to make her a villain.”

	Old Hollywood is a key influence and part of the fabric of the film, classic clips are spliced, Bette Davis on a poster looks on in key scenes.

	Evans grew up in a deeply religious household where films produced after the sixties were forbidden. Instead, she spent her teenage years discovering Charlie Chaplin, Greta Garbo, Alfred Hitchcock and the women of Hollywood’s studio era.

	“I was a 14 year old who didn’t know who Miley Cyrus was, didn’t know what ‘Twilight’ was,” she laughs. “I was in Texas watching these old movies.”

	“Gone With the Wind” proved especially formative. For the director, Scarlett O’Hara’s determination became an early model of female strength.

	“I saw Joan Crawford and Bette Davis and these women, and I was like: they have voice,” said Evans. “Those aren’t women you want to pass in a dark alley. They are forces to be reckoned with.”

	Growing up without what she felt was a strong cultural inheritance, classic Hollywood became one.

	“This is my culture. This is my mythology. This is my American mythos.”

	That fascination runs throughout the story. Classical cinema is a dream world for Marie and Luna to imagine themselves into.

	She describes herself as “deeply impressionistic” rather than realist.“Cinema has to be hope,” she said. “I want to show people better than who they are.”
	



	

	



	Alongside Old Hollywood, Evans cites Sofia Coppola’s “The Virgin Suicides,” Robert Altman’s “3 Women,” Ingmar Bergman’s “Persona,” Martin Scorsese’s “Taxi Driver” and Warhol’s films as important influences. While Coppola shaped the intimacy between the girls, “Persona” informed one of the film’s sexual sequences, and “Taxi Driver” became a reference point for imagining a story from the perspective of a character like Jodie Foster’s Iris.

	“There’s such a specific motif for me in this movie of the sweat and then the glitter,” she said. Cinematographer Laura Guiteras runs with this as we return frequently to light bouncing off the sheen the sweat gives upon the characters faces.

	Originally intended to shoot in New Mexico, production relocated to Tulsa, Oklahoma after costs became prohibitive. The city’s Art Deco architecture gave the production a welcome location nod to Hollywood’s golden age.

	“It feels like a ghost town,” she explained. “There’s such untouched Art Deco.”

	The film’s intimacy also emerged from Evans’ directing process.

	She encouraged the actors to remain in character for extended takes asking them to continue inhabiting the moment while the camera rolled.

	“The crew called them ‘breathing moments,'” she said. “I’d say, ‘You’re not going to hear cut. I want you to live as the character.'”

	The approach generated a significant amount of footage resulting in a first cut running around two and a half hours before she and editor Benjamin Rodriguez Jr., a frequent Paul Schrader collaborator, reduced it to its final 90-minute form.

	Ultimately, the director hopes “Pretty Babies” encourages audiences to see past the identities imposed upon its characters.

	“I really hope they feel the essence and the depth and the wonder of their own soul watching it,” she said. “That they’re not just a stereotype. That there is immense complexity within them.”

schema.headline: ‘Pretty Babies’ Director Tyler-Marie Evans on Sex Work, Female Friendship and Finding Humanity Beyond Stereotypes

title: Locarno Takeaways: A Charming Olivia Wilde, Navigating an Industry Crunch and One Reason Why There Should Be More Women Filmmakers
description: Unspooling over Aug. 5-15, this year’s Locarno Film Festival broke records for industry attendance and its temperatures, Switzerland enduring its ho
body:
Unspooling over Aug. 5-15, this year’s Locarno Film Festival broke records for industry attendance and its temperatures, Switzerland enduring its hottest summer since records began in 1864. Led by an ebullient Olivia Wilde, charged by the breakout success of “The Invite,” Locarno Pro delivered a telling take on the world’s arthouse crunch with the sector courting venture capital to fill the breach of contracting finance from traditional sources.
	

	These and other industry takeaways fom this year’s Locarno Film Festival.  


	Why Stars Attend Locarno


	Olivia Wilde charmed unveiling to a Piazza Grande audience “The Invite,” on its European premiere, to an 8,000 audience. Zoe Saldaña, who also received a tribute, explained why she was bothered by political questions. Another Locarno honoree, James Gray, presenting “Paper Tiger,” was in fine fettle delivering a stomping interview with Variety, calling AI “worthless” and arguing “young people won’t stand for it.” Monica Bellucci declared she’d never done anything like her role in “Ketticè”: “On set in my pyjamas with a knife in my hand and slippers on my feet.” Europe’s biggest mid-summer film event, “Locarno offers prestige, elegance and plenty of press attention at what is a much less crowded selection than most festivals in the awards season corridor,” Stuart Ford, at AGC Intl., told Variety last year when he brought “Kiss of the Spider Woman” to Locarno. That reason still stands as Locarno’s star presence builds ever more.  

	Buzz Titles

	Variety called “Objet a,” an Oscilloscope U.S. pick-up from Ann Oren (“Piaff”), “a wickedly kinky curiosity.” “Hearing” (“gorgeous, secretive”), Swedish-Danish Maria Back’s “Brave New Love” (an “emotionally intelligent, gently wry character drama”) and Felix Randau’s “I Is Another” (“a handsomely upholstered psychological thriller”) also came in for Variety praise. As did German Isabelle Stever’s “I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming,” “stark surprising.” Elsewhere, Argentinean Alessandra Sanguinetti’s “The Illusion of an Everlasting Summer” – dreamy, grounded,” said Variety — had plenty of fans. 
	

	Locarno’s Industry Value

	“Who is full of hope?” moderator A.C. Coppens, The Catalysts founder, asked a packed audience at Locarno’s Step-In think tank’s opening panel after Stephen Follows damning analysis of algorithm-driven decision-making in a Step-In introduction. Only two hands went up from audience members. Locarno Pro itself drives to identify opportunities during good times and industry malaise. “When we did Step-In before the pandemic, we asked what the film industry would look like in five years time. Now that’s impossible. Step-In is anticipating one-to-two years max because things are moving so fast,” says Locarno Pro director Markus Duffner. That said, Locarno in 2026, supplied multiple suggestions for ways forward for the international independent sector. 

	Co-Production: The Industry’s Get Out of Jail Card

	One, without doubt, is co-production. “Our aim is to build projects around international collaboration from their earliest stages,” Portuguese producer Ana Sofia Nunes told Variety at Match Me! Locarno’s large networking event. Most producers there agreed. Indeed, international co-production was highlighted by 12 of 20 Match Me! producers who talked to Variety about their business model, followed by genre production (three) and non-theatrical distribution (two). Match Me! can furthers their aims, notes Duffner, citing Chile’s Equeco and Italy’s Dispàrte, behind 2026 Locarno Piazza Grande premiere “The Chilean,” who met at Match Me!   

	Venture Capital Investment

	There’s a new kid in town: venture capital investment, drawn to the Swiss Festival by a second Locarno Investment Community held over Aug. 6-9. Investors are discovering the value of the movie business. Why? “Because we need them,” answers Alexandra Lebret, ex MD of the European Producers Club, now co-heading investor Together Fund, co-financed by the E.U.’s MediaInvest fund. Europe’s film industry now faces a triple-whammy: Shrinking broadcaster, international distributor and now state aid, and selective schemes — think France’s Cinémas du Monde are “very, very competitive,” said Lebret. “Producers will have to produce with less. There is more space for private investors. The whole system needs to adapt to first a new reality and secondly, to new players that are coming and will change the rules,” Lebret forecast. “Private investment is one answer to diminishing or evolving public funding for art films,” says Duffner. 
	

	Genre Build

	Of projects shopped at Match Me!, “The Girl Who Bled Women,” from Brazil’s Movioca and turning on a girl’s determination not to lose her virginity in an arranged marriage, was cast as a survival thriller. “Half of the world, from France’s Belladonna Films, is a “contemporary genre film with elements of comedy,” said producer Gabriel Jumel. “The Educator,” produced by Montenegro’s Adriatic Western, weighs in as  a “fresh take on the Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde Smith,” producer Ivan Marinóvic told Variety. In all, 12 of the top projects presented by 35 producers at Match Me! were genre films or had distinct genre elements. “Most genre, not only elevated genre but more commercial genre, makes some political statement, and Locarno, with Giona [A. Nazzaro’s] editorial line as artistic director, has embraced more and more these kind of films and that can be seen in Locarno Pro lineups,” says Duffner.  

	The Need for More Films by Women

	The industry could also do with more films by women. “I don’t know if you’ve come across those little plaques that you sometimes see in offices that say: ‘You don’t have to be mad to work here, but it helps.’ The film version is: ‘You don’t have to be a white, cisgendered, not-disabled, middle class urban man to work here, but it helps,’” Doris Ruth Eikhof, at the University of Glasgow and Design Otherwise said. She went on to cite German film data that suggested that even from just a business point of view, that is short-sighted: Films produced by men need €41 ($48) to sell one cinema ticket, women just €13 ($15). When they are selected, films by women are typically more successful, have a longer festival run and win more awards, Eikhof said.

	Arthouse’s Generational Makeover

	At the turn of the century, arthouse theaters in Europe were frequented by ageing baby boomers. Now, ”we see a huge young audience coming to our cinema,” Joyce Palmers, at Antwerp’s De Cinema repertory theater, said at Step-In’s opening panel. That may have two knock-ons. One most certainly: De Cinema’s young audience “loves to see classics.” A central panel at Locarno’s Heritage Monday identified classic film exhibition as one, however niche, future for cinema. Also, arthouse movies and directors breaking out around the world most often share the interest of a younger audience, making films of contemporary relevance, political and social point and authenticity. Notably, upscale European films may be skewing younger. Seven of the 11 projects at Alliance 4 Development, Locarno’s platform for bigger projects, have young protagonists or as co-leads.   
	

	Moving Beyond Nuclear Families

	Increasingly, titles are certainly capturing a younger generation Zeitgeist. Multiple titles also chart for Millennials and the Gen Z the evolution of bedrock relations beyond those of nuclear families. Ghanaian Artei Armar’s “Our Time Will Come” trails two orphans who move to Accra to find chosen family. ‘The Illusion of an Everlasting Summer” records cousins Guille and Belinda over 25 years as they grow up, fall in love, raise children and slowly drift apart. “Kinship, whether by blood or affinity, is redefined for a modern world,” writes Variety of “Our Time Will Come”, which could be said of two notable titles in Locarno’s Spanish Film Previews which again chart far more fluid bedrock relations: Diego Llorente’s “How the Lights Get In” and Paloma Zapata’s “Juliette & Camille.”

	Family Arthouse

	Or sales agents and distributors are turning to family arthouse. Kids and family pics are driving an ever larger part Locarno’s business dealings. In one move, Locarno Kids title “Mu-ki-ra,” a flamboyant animated feature and political allegory from Colombian creative powerhouse Estefanía Piñeres Duque and “Decorado” producer Chelo Loureiro, was brought to market by Latido Films. And in another, Patra Spanou Films closed world sales rights to Rodrigo Plá’s “Los Nuevos” after its world premiere at Locarno. “An increasing number of international distributors are handling family arthouse for broader audiences, and come to Locarno to focus on Locarno Kids, which now has a lot of international and world premieres too,” Duffner comments. 

	The Business

	Locarno sparked a bevy of U.S. pickups and a slew of sales agent deals on movies in main international competition and Piazza Grande titles. 

	Just some of the deals at Locarno 2026 announced by Variety: 

	*Ahead of Locarno world premiere, Oscilloscope Laboratories acquires Ann Oren’s “Objet a,” which went on to spark rave reviews at the Swiss festival.

	*Cinetic Media swooped on North America sales rights to “Manhunt,” a Locarno Main Competition contender. Aspect Ratio has taken international sales rights.

	*”Bloody Tennis” sold to Shudder for the U.S. in a CAA deal, with the expose of elite sport extremes closing major territories — Australia (Umbrella Entertainment), Italy (Plaion Pictures), Japan (Extreme Film) and Scandinavia (Njutafilms) — in the run-up to Locarno. The Playmaker Munich and Augenschein Sales handled international deals.
	

	*Hong Sangsoo’s “Nowhere to Lay My Eyes” landed at Cinema Guild ahead of its Locarno Premiere 

	*Heretic pounced on Denis Còté’s awaited “Nobody’s Violence,” in a mid-July deal. According to many critics it proved worth the waiting with Côté, “proving once again to be an inimitable observer of the human condition,” said iCs.

	*Fandango Sales picked up explosive Locarno Premiere “The Chilean,” a ‘70s-set militant-left thriller from top Chilean scribe-helmer Sergio Castro-San Martín, creator of “La Jauría.”

	*”Small Talk,” a nuanced take on Switzerland’s last finishing school, was boarded by France’s Urban Sales. 

	*And “La Koreana,” a banner new talent title from Spain, was brought to market at Locarno by producers Lazona Zinema and Sirimiri, headed by “20,000 Species of Bees” director Estibaliz Urresola.

	*In other deals unveiled just after the Locarno lineup announcement in July, Brazilian erotic thriller “The Riverbank” was boarded by Premium Films/MPM Premium. 

	*While Bendita Film Sales swooped on Locarno-bound “Donkey Princess,” from “The Wolf House” directors León & Cociña;

	*In other trading, Low Light Films took Basil Da Cunha’s “O Jacaré,” a celebration of Lisbon’s vibrant Reboleira district.

	*And Isabelle Stever’s Locarno main competition title, “I Rarely Wake Up Dreaming,” produced by Tom Tykwer, was picked up for world sales by France’s Outplay Films

	*Heretic also secured sales rights on Lê Bảo’s “Hearing,” praised by Variety as a “sensuous, intuitive mood piece.” 

	*Dario Albertini’s “Armony,” bowing at Locarno’s Piazza Grande, secured Swiss distribution with Xenix.

	*Italy-Based Lights On snapped up Colombia’s “In All My Journeys I Am Returning.”

	*”The Days Off,” Lucila Mariani’s dreamlike Argentine debut, found a sales agent at Inwave Films.

                          I Need Her to Bear the Cost of Spousal Support!!!
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              August 14, 2026
                            10:40 AM PDT
                                                                            
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Abby Elliott's estranged husband wants her to cut him monthly checks ... as their bitter divorce heats up and they fight over finances.
      
    
            According to new legal docs, obtained by TMZ, Bill Kennedy filed a response to her divorce petition ... and he's requesting spousal support.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Bill, who was married to Abby for a decade, is also asking to block the court's ability to award spousal support to her. He also asks that Abby pay his attorneys' fees.
      
    
            He wants joint legal and physical custody of their two children ... 5-year-old Edith and 3-year-old William Kennedy.
      

            There's a lot of information Bill doesn't seem to have at this time ... he says the date of separation is "TBD" -- while Abby claimed in her own filing it was July 8, 2026. Bill's also asking the judge for more time to determine what constitutes his separate property and debts ... writing that they are "unknown at this time."
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            We broke the story ... Abby filed for divorce last month -- citing "irreconcilable differences."
      
    
            Abby also requested spousal support and asked to terminate the court's ability to award him any. She also wants him to foot the bill for her attorney’s fees.
      
    
            Fans will recognize Abby from her on-camera roles on "The Bear" and from "Saturday Night Live" back in the day ... while Bill's a behind-the-camera creative -- with writing credits on "House of Cards" and "The Morning Show."

Cardi B to BIA
                          I Got Something in the Tuck for You!!!

            Cardi B is calling BS on BIA, claiming her diss track was all true ... and warning her rap rival she's got plenty of dirt tucked away.
      
    
            Cardi came out swinging in a Spaces chat on X ... repeatedly demanding, "What's true?" before launching into a laundry list of claims about BIA.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            She claims BIA desperately wanted to be friends before their beef and repeatedly sent word through mutual friends that she had no problem with Cardi ... and Cardi says she's got recordings to prove it.
      

            Cardi also denied BIA's claim she slept with someone to become gang-affiliated ... saying she "turned blue" at 16 and never had sex with anyone to do so.
      
    
      
        
              
    
    
            She then ripped BIA's street cred before issuing one final warning -- she's got "something in the tuck" for BIA and other female rappers ... and teased she could unleash it on her third album.
      
    
            So much for keeping the beef on wax ... Cardi certainly had a few things she wanted to get off her chest.
